catalog_quote: ACCENT (8) For the accent of the words the following notes may help. (9) (a) in words composed of a v-c-v the accent is on the last vowel, which is long. E.g. abaa (father), obwoo (net), oboo (lungs) etc. . . . The verbs make an exception. E.g. uru (to wonder), ono (to cough), umu (to cover), etc. . . . . (10) (b) in words with a c-v-c the stress is on the only vowel they have. E.g. bol (handle), ret (wound), tic (work), cam (food), etc. . . . (11) (c) in words with a v-c-v-c the accent is on the last vowel. E.g., olik (bat), obwol (muchroom), olam (fig tree), ogwal (frog), etc. . . . (12) (d) in words with a c-v-c-v the accent is on the stem-vowel. E.g., geno (to hope), balo (to spoil), jago (sub-chief), banya (debt) ... (13) (e) in words with a v-c-v-c-v the accent is on the central vowel. E.g., oboro (shell), aboro (eight), okado (bee-eater) ... (14) The position of the accent remain…

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Malandra 1955, classification morphological): accent by word shape, e.g. V-CV nouns (prefix a-/o- + stem) accented on the last (stem) vowel, CVC on the only vowel, verbs an exception. Tucker & Bryan's group-level rule 'stress on the Stem, never on Prefixes or Suffixes' is the same type (root/stem stress) and matches Malandra's prefix-unstressed pattern; it adds (refinement, group-level) a link between stress and vowel length in S. Lwo and says nothing about Malandra's verb exception. Statement is made for the four Nilotic heads jointly with Acoli-Lango as the S. Lwo exemplar, not for Acoli alone; snippets only, so surrounding qualifications may be missing.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Nilotic languages jointly (Dinka, Nuer, N. Lwo = Shilluk, S. Lwo exemplified by Acoli-Lango): word stress falls on the stem and never on prefixes or suffixes, i.e. morphologically (root-) determined; for S. Lwo (Acoli-Lango, Alur, Luo) the authors add that stress seems related to vowel length, and that Acoli-Lango has only two length degrees with truly long vowels mostly in final open syllables (behaving disyllabically).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged 'As a general rule'; 'some relationship between stress and vowel length in S. LWO (see § 14 (i))' (cross-referenced passage not fully recovered; footnote ² to the Acoli-Lango length sentence not recovered).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan treat Acoli under the 'S. LWO' head of the Nilotic chapter ('S. LWO: examples from ACOLI-LANGO, ALUR, Kenya LUO'; informants J. B. Akot, ACOLI and N. E. Opio, LANGO, ACOLI); the stress rule is stated for the four Nilotic heads jointly (Dinka [Bor], Nuer [Western], N. Lwo [Shilluk], S. Lwo [Acoli-Lango]) and the vowel-length remarks specifically for ACOLI-LANGO. The catalog record (Malandra 1955) describes Acholi of Uganda.

sources.quote: No word-stress rule given. 'Acooli is a tone language, exhibiting a low tone, a high tone, a falling tone, a rising tone, a downstep high tone and a double downstep high tone which contrast on phonetic level. However, a low toneme and a high toneme are posited in underlying representations.' (p.7). 'Acooli vowels have no distinctive opposition of length in lexicon. However, phonologically distinctive long vowels occur in forms which are derived through morphosyntactic processes' (p.4; e.g. maato 'to drink'). Only mention of stress is fn.: 'Vowel sandhi occurs in unstressed vowels.' Also: 'Craz
